topics.topic: How SQLite database and auxiliary files stay anchored to the held-open data directory
questions: How must SQLite open the database and its journal so they remain anchored to the checked, held-open data directory if that directory's pathname or an ancestor is renamed or replaced after start?
How must SQLite be made to open the database and auxiliary files relative to the held-open data-directory descriptor, so replacement or renaming of the configured pathname cannot redirect it?
How must SQLite be made to open the database and its journal if an ancestor renames or replaces the data-directory pathname after start?

quotes:
The data directory itself is reached as A17 rule 1 reaches the configuration file, component by
   component with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and opened for reading at its last component.

Every file the store opens itself is opened relative to the data directory
   it holds open from the start, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW`,
   never first asking whether the flag exists (A20 rule 3); a link met so later
   makes that store call fail, writing no record (rule 3).

The database file and its journal are opened by
   SQLite, which Python cannot ask to refuse a link — the journal being every
   file SQLite itself creates beside the database under the database's name,
   in whatever journal mode the database file holds; the kernel sets none and
   checks none; the start's check covers them, and the kernel does not watch them after it: in a private directory
   only the kernel's user or root can place a link, and either can change any
   record directly, so a link gives them nothing more (owner, 2026-10-18).
judgement.divergence: One implementation makes SQLite resolve the database and auxiliary files through the held-open directory, so pathname replacement does not redirect storage; another gives SQLite the original pathname, so a later rename or replacement can redirect auxiliary-file access, which the owner and store callers notice through changed, missing, or split persistent state.
judgement.why: The rules require descriptor-relative opening for files the store opens itself but do not say how SQLite's independently opened files remain anchored after pathname changes.

topics.topic: Required behavior and testing when Linux sandbox, namespace, or limit facilities are unavailable
questions: Do the mandatory A03 checks and defined limit-setting failure still apply when Linux lacks a required namespace, limit, or sandbox facility, or does A20 make those cases untested and behaviorally undefined?
Must startup detect missing Linux namespace and limit facilities through the required sandbox probe and refuse to start, or is behavior on such a host wholly undefined with no required test?
On Linux lacking a namespace or limit needed by A03, must the sandbox probe detect the failure and make startup refuse, or is behavior deliberately undefined with no such test required?

quotes:
The kernel checks at start, before recovery and before the surface opens,
   that `bubblewrap` is present and that one probe execution succeeds; without
   both it does not start, and says why.

A limit
   that cannot be set means the code is not loaded and the execution is
   `crashed`.

A Linux that lacks a
   facility these rules use — `O_PATH`, `O_NOFOLLOW`, the namespaces and limits
   of A03 — is unsupported as another system is: the kernel neither tests the
   host nor defines what it does on an unsupported one.
judgement.why: A03 mandates detected behavior for failed sandbox facilities and limits, while A20 says those same missing facilities are neither tested nor behaviorally defined.

topics.topic: Whether a store operation encountering a post-start symlink may leave any published file or filesystem write
questions: May a store call that later encounters a symbolic link leave a published but unreferenced file as rule 3 generally permits, or must this failure leave no filesystem write at all as the required test says?
May a store call that encounters a symlink leave a complete unreferenced published file, or must it leave no filesystem write at all?
What happens when a symlink is present after start at a rename destination, spool position, temporary-file name, or cleanup target that the store operates on without opening it?

quotes:
A call that fails writes and changes no record; the only
   trace it can leave is a published file no record names, which nothing reads:
   a spooled file is replaced at its position, value bytes are reused by equal
   bytes until the next start removes them (rule 4).

A symbolic link in the value area stops the start; one placed there after
   the start makes the store call that meets it fail with nothing written.
judgement.why: The normative rule permits a failed call to leave a published unreferenced file, while the required test demands that this symlink failure leave nothing written.

topics.topic: Starting directory for component-by-component traversal of an absolute path
questions: From which opened directory descriptor does component-by-component traversal of an absolute configuration or credential path begin?

When component-by-component traversal receives an absolute path, is its starting directory the filesystem root, the kernel's working directory after empty components are skipped, or is the path refused?

quotes:
Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW` — a directory on the way with `O_PATH` as well, so a directory
   the kernel's user may only pass through is passed; a relative path starts
   at the kernel's working directory; empty and `.` components are skipped,
   and `..` is opened as any other component — it names the parent of the
   directory reached so far and is never a link; the host is Linux (A20 rule 3), so no code asks whether a flag
   exists and there is no mode without it —, and the checks and the read
   use that one opened file, so the file checked is the file read.
judgement.divergence: One implementation begins an absolute path at the filesystem root and opens the intended file; another begins at the working directory after skipping the leading empty component, or refuses the path, so the owner observes a different configuration or credential being read or startup/request refusal.
judgement.why: The traversal rule identifies the base for relative paths but never identifies the starting descriptor or refusal behavior for absolute paths.

topics.topic: How to handle a data-directory path with no remaining traversable component
questions: What happens when `data_directory` has no component left after skipping, such as `.`, `./`, an empty path, or `/` after its empty components: is the starting directory itself opened and checked, or is the configuration refused?

topics.topic: Which SQLite journal modes are compatible with the unconditional transaction atomicity guarantee
questions: Is every SQLite journal mode accepted while the no-partial-record guarantee remains unconditional, or must incompatible modes be refused or replaced?
